newsitem.title: GERMANY: TENNIS-TOUR BOSS HITS AT GRAND SLAM CUP SWITCH.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-TOUR BOSS HITS AT GRAND SLAM CUP SWITCH.

text.p: The head of the men's tennis tour attacked the controversial Grand Slam Cup on Friday, saying organisers were being selfish and destructive with new plans for the game's most lucrative tournament.

Mark Miles, chief of the Association of Tennis Professionals (ATP), which runs most of the world's tournaments, said moving the Munich event from December to earlier in the season from 1997 would upset the sport's crowded calendar.
"It's a self-centred decision," Miles said at the Stuttgart Open. "It is putting another big event in the middle of a crowded season. It puts an obstacle to the flow of events."

The Munich tournament, which pays out prize money of 3.75 million pounds sterling ($6 million), brings together the top performers from the four Grand Slam events: Wimbledon and the French, Australian and U.S. Opens.
The event has caused a stir in the game since it was set up in 1990 by the four organisers of the Grand Slams which operate outside of the ATP.

At first some players said the money on offer was obscene and refused to play. Although few players can resist the cash on offer now, ATP officials, who organise their own season-ending world championship, tend to regard it as an exhibition event.

The Cup has been played for its first six seasons after the ATP Tour has finished. But next year organisers plan to have the event in September, shortly after the U.S. Open -- the last grand slam of the year. The move is almost certain to raise the profile of the event and the ATP is not happy.
Miles said it would be hard for about 11 Tour events which take place around the Cup to get major players to attend their tournaments.
"It can't be good news for any of them," Miles said. "Our position is that it could have a potential negative effect -- not just in events in Asia but also in Europe."
